sections.b: The Psalter opens with two psalms that have no titles, framed by the word "Happy" (Psalm 1:1; Psalm 2:12). Psalm 1 sets the way of the LORD's teaching against the way of the wicked; Psalm 2 sets the LORD's anointed king against the rebel nations. The Talmud counts them as one psalm (Bavli Berakhot 9b–10a), and some manuscripts of Acts 13:33 call Psalm 2 "the first psalm." Most scholars think the editors placed them here to tell readers how to read the whole book: as instruction to murmur over day and night, and as a book of hope in God's king. Words link the two: the "murmuring" of Psalm 1:2 and Psalm 2:1, the "road" that is "lost" in Psalm 1:6 and Psalm 2:12.

sections.h: Book I and the psalms of David (Psalms 3–41)
sections.b: Book I is almost entirely "of David": every psalm from 3 to 41 has his name in the title except 10 and 33 (and 10 is the second half of Psalm 9). It is full of individual laments, prayers of one person beset by enemies, sickness or false charges (3–7; 13; 17), with hymns among them (8) and an entrance liturgy (15). It uses God's name YHWH far more than Elohim. Many of the titles point to David's flight from Saul or Absalom (3:0; 7:0; 18:0; 34:0). Read together, Book I gives the voice of a king who suffers and trusts, which Jewish readers heard as David's and the New Testament also as the Messiah's.
sections.refs: Psalm 3:0; Psalm 7:0; Psalm 13:1–6; Psalm 18:0; Psalm 34:0; Psalm 41:13

common: Psalms 1 and 2 were placed together on purpose as the introduction to the whole Psalter.
uncommon: Some scholars think Psalm 1 was written specifically as a preface for the finished book, after the exile.

sections.h: Psalm 2: the LORD and his anointed
sections.b: Psalm 2 is the first place in the Psalter where the word mashiach, "anointed one," appears (Psalm 2:2). In its first setting it is the king of David's line, crowned on Zion and adopted as God's son (Psalm 2:6–7; compare 2 Samuel 7:14). After the kings, Jewish readers looked to a future son of David: the Psalms of Solomon 17, a Qumran scroll (4Q174) and the Talmud (Bavli Sukkah 52a) apply Psalm 2 to the Messiah, while Rashi, against Christian use, reads it of David. The New Testament applies it to Jesus at his baptism (Mark 1:11), in the apostles' prayer (Acts 4:25–28), at his resurrection (Acts 13:33), in Hebrews (Hebrews 1:5) and in Revelation's iron rod (Revelation 19:15). The debated "kiss the son" (Psalm 2:12) is discussed in a variant there.
sections.refs: Psalm 2:1–12; 2 Samuel 7:14; Mark 1:11; Acts 4:25–28; Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Revelation 19:15

common: Psalm 2 is one of the main Old Testament texts for the New Testament's claim that Jesus is the Messiah and Son of God.
uncommon: Some scholars think Psalm 2 was composed after the exile as a messianic poem, not for a real coronation.

sections.h: The king in Psalm 2 and Psalms 9–10
sections.b: Psalm 2 shows how Judah thought of its king: chosen by the LORD, installed on Zion, given the nations as his inheritance. The promises are far bigger than any real king's power, which is why scholars speak of an ideal of kingship and believers of a hope still to be fulfilled. Psalms 9–10 widen the picture: the LORD himself is king forever (Psalm 9:7; Psalm 10:16), seated on his throne to judge, and his rule is measured by how he treats the orphan and the oppressed (Psalm 10:14; Psalm 10:18).

The decree of Psalm 2:7, "You are my son. This day I have fathered you," is spoken on the day of the king's crowning and echoes God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 89:26–27). In its setting it is adoption: the king becomes God's son by appointment. The New Testament hears it at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration (Mark 1:11; Mark 9:7), applies "this day" to the resurrection (Acts 13:33) and uses it to set the Son above the angels (Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5). Later creeds read "begotten" of the Son's eternal relation to the Father; Jewish interpreters keep the royal, adoptive sense.
sections.refs: Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 89:26–27; Mark 1:11; Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5

sections.b: Most of Psalms 3–17 are laments of one person: a fugitive king (Psalm 3), a slandered man (Psalm 4), an accused worshiper at daybreak (Psalm 5), a sick man (Psalm 6), a man under false charges (Psalm 7; Psalm 17), the poor under oppression (Psalm 10), a faithful remnant among liars (Psalm 12). Psalm 13 is the textbook case: four "how long?" questions, a plea, and a turn to trust. Many of them change mood suddenly (Psalm 6:8; Psalm 13:5), which scholars explain as a word of assurance received in worship or as the work of faith in the act of praying. They give the sufferer permission to protest to God without leaving him.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the sleep thread in Book I's opening
claude.body: My own observation: Psalms 3, 4, 6, 13 and 17 are linked by sleep and waking. The fugitive lies down and wakes (3:5); the slandered man sleeps in peace (4:8); the sick man floods his bed (6:6); the forgotten man fears the sleep of death (13:3); the accused man expects to be satisfied when he wakes (17:15). Arranged in this order, the night moves from trust, through tears and the fear of death, to a waking that may be more than morning. Commentators note the morning and evening settings of single psalms; reading the sequence as a deliberate progression is my suggestion.

sections.b: Three early psalms show the range of the Psalter's thought about death. In Psalm 6:5 the sick man argues that in Sheol no one praises God, so God should keep him alive. In Psalm 9:13 and Psalm 9:17 death is a city with gates, and the wicked "go back" to Sheol. In Psalm 16:10 the psalmist is sure God will not leave him to Sheol or let his loyal one see the Pit, and Psalm 16:11 speaks of delights that never end. Scholars debate whether Psalm 16 hopes for rescue from early death or for life beyond it; Acts 2:27–31 reads it of Jesus' resurrection, and Christians later linked it with his descent to the dead.

common: The Old Testament's early picture of Sheol is a shadowy place where all the dead go, not a place of punishment.
uncommon: Some scholars (Dahood) find a hope of life after death already in early psalms like Psalm 16 and Psalm 17.

sections.b: In the first laments of the Psalter, hesed is the ground of hope. The worshiper enters God's house only "by the greatness of your loyal love" (Psalm 5:7); the sick man asks to be saved "for the sake of your loyal love" (Psalm 6:4); the forgotten man trusts in it when nothing has changed (Psalm 13:5); the accused asks God to make his acts of loyal love wonderful, as at the exodus (Psalm 17:7). The chasid, the person of loyal love, is the one God sets apart (Psalm 4:3) and the one whose disappearance is lamented (Psalm 12:1).
sections.refs: Psalm 4:3; Psalm 5:7; Psalm 6:4; Psalm 12:1; Psalm 13:5; Psalm 17:7

sections.b: Book I of the Psalms prefers God's personal name, YHWH, "the LORD" (Psalm 1:2), and uses it far more than Elohim, "God"; Psalms 42–83 reverse the pattern, which is why the twin Psalms 14 and 53 differ in their name for God. Other names appear: Adonai, "the Lord" (Psalm 2:4), Adonenu, "our Lord" (Psalm 8:1), Elyon, "Most High" (Psalm 7:17; Psalm 9:2), the title first used by Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18), and "my King and my God" (Psalm 5:2).
sections.refs: Psalm 1:2; Psalm 2:4; Psalm 5:2; Psalm 7:17; Psalm 8:1; Psalm 9:2; Psalm 14:2; Psalm 53:2

sections.b: Psalm 1 opens the Psalter with the person whose delight is "the law of the LORD" and who murmurs over it day and night (Psalm 1:2), echoing Joshua 1:8. Here torah is more than commandments: it is God's whole teaching, and many scholars think the editors placed Psalm 1 first to make the Psalter itself a torah to be studied. The Midrash on Psalms compares the five books of the Psalter with the five books of Moses. Psalm 15 then lists what the LORD's guests must do, a summary of the law that the Talmud says David reduced to eleven commands (Bavli Makkot 24a).

Psalm 1 is the Psalter's statement of the two ways: the road of the righteous, which the LORD knows, and the road of the wicked, which will be lost (Psalm 1:6). The images are a planted tree and blowing chaff (Psalm 1:3–4). Psalm 2 ends with the same warning to the kings, "you will be lost on your road" (Psalm 2:12). The same choice runs through Deuteronomy 30:15–20, Jeremiah 17:5–8 and Jesus' narrow and wide roads (Matthew 7:13–14).

sections.h: Psalm 8: the night sky and human honor
sections.b: Psalm 8 is a hymn of creation that looks up at the moon and stars, "the work of your fingers," and asks why God cares for mortals (Psalm 8:3–4). Its answer echoes Genesis 1:26–28: humans are made only a little less than God and given rule over the animals (Psalm 8:5–8). The enemies silenced by babies' voices (Psalm 8:2) may recall old pictures of God defeating chaos at creation, here replaced by the weakest voices. Paul and Hebrews read the rule of Psalm 8:6 as fulfilled in Christ (1 Corinthians 15:27; Hebrews 2:8).

Psalm 8:5 is the Psalter's comment on the image of God: humans are made "only a little less than God" and crowned with glory and majesty, as kings are crowned. The Hebrew elohim can mean God or heavenly beings, and the Greek, followed by Hebrews 2:7, has "angels." Either way the psalm gives every human being royal honor and responsibility over creation.

In Psalm 8:4, "son of man" (ben adam) means simply a human being, parallel to "mortal." Hebrews 2:6–9 reads the verse of Jesus, the human being who for a while was made lower than the angels and is now crowned. The phrase is the same one Ezekiel is called by and is close to the "one like a son of man" of Daniel 7:13.

Psalm 16:10–11 is the Old Testament text the apostles used most for the resurrection: "you will not leave my life to Sheol; you will not allow your loyal one to see the Pit" (the Greek has "decay"). Peter argues that David died and was buried, so the words point to the Messiah (Acts 2:25–32); Paul makes the same case (Acts 13:35–37). Psalm 17:15, "When I wake up, I will be filled with the sight of your form," was read by many Jewish and Christian interpreters as waking from death to see God. Many critical scholars read both as hope for rescue in this life; others see an early hope of life beyond death.

common: The New Testament reads Psalm 16:10 as a prophecy of Jesus' resurrection.
uncommon: Some scholars think Psalm 16:10 originally expected only that God would keep the psalmist from an early death.

sections.b: Psalm 15 is an entrance liturgy: worshipers arriving at the sanctuary ask who may be the LORD's guest, and the answer lists honest speech, kindness to neighbors, loyalty to the God-fearing, kept oaths, loans without interest and no bribes (Psalm 15:1–5). It says nothing about sacrifice or ritual cleanness. Psalm 24:3–6 and Isaiah 33:14–16 have the same form. Psalm 5:7 and Psalm 11:4 picture the LORD's temple both on Zion and in heaven.

Psalms 3–17 introduce most of the technical words of the titles. Mizmor, "a psalm" (Psalm 3:0), is a song sung to strings; tefillah, "a prayer" (Psalm 17:0). Lamnatseach, "for the music director" (Psalm 4:0), the Greek read as "for the end." Shiggaion (Psalm 7:0) and miktam (Psalm 16:0) are unexplained. Instruments and tunes are named: stringed instruments (Psalm 4:0), flutes (Psalm 5:0), the sheminith, "the eighth" (Psalm 6:0; Psalm 12:0), the gittith (Psalm 8:0) and muth-labben (Psalm 9:0). Two titles name events: David's flight from Absalom (Psalm 3:0) and "the words of Cush, a Benjaminite" (Psalm 7:0), whom the Talmud identifies as Saul (Bavli Moed Katan 16b).

sections.h: Selah and the music of the early psalms
sections.b: Selah, kept untranslated, first appears in Psalm 3:2 and occurs 71 times in the Psalms and three times in Habakkuk 3. The Greek rendered it diapsalma, perhaps an instrumental interlude; the Targum and Jerome's Hebrew Psalter took it as "forever." Higgaion (Psalm 9:16), from the verb for murmuring, may be a quiet musical passage. The titles of Psalms 4–12 name strings, flutes, "the eighth" (perhaps an eight-stringed lyre or a lower register, compare 1 Chronicles 15:21) and the gittith.
sections.refs: Psalm 3:2; Psalm 4:0; Psalm 5:0; Psalm 6:0; Psalm 8:0; Psalm 9:16; Habakkuk 3:3; 1 Chronicles 15:21

sections.b: Christian tradition, from Cassiodorus in the 500s, counts seven penitential psalms: Psalm 6, Psalm 32, Psalm 38, Psalm 51, Psalm 102, Psalm 130 and Psalm 143. Psalm 6 is first, though it never names a sin: it asks God not to discipline in anger (Psalm 6:1). The seven were prayed in Lent, at confession and at deathbeds through the Middle Ages, and Luther's first printed book (1517) expounded them. Psalm 7:12 also speaks of turning back: "If one does not turn back..."

sections.h: God the judge in Psalms 7, 9 and 17
sections.b: The accused of Psalm 7 and Psalm 17 bring their cases to God as judge, swearing innocence and asking for a verdict "from before you" (Psalm 17:2). Ancient Israel allowed such oaths at the sanctuary when no witnesses could decide (Exodus 22:8–11; 1 Kings 8:31–32). Psalm 9 pictures God seated on the throne to judge the world fairly and to be a high tower for the downtrodden (Psalm 9:7–9). "My righteousness" in these psalms means being in the right in a dispute, not sinlessness.

The early psalms are full of the poor: the afflicted, the humble, the needy, the downtrodden, the helpless, the orphan. God is their high tower (Psalm 9:9), the one who avenges their blood (Psalm 9:12), the orphan's helper (Psalm 10:14), who rises when they groan (Psalm 12:5) and is their shelter (Psalm 14:6). The wicked prey on them as a lion on its prey (Psalm 10:8–10) and devour them like bread (Psalm 14:4). The written Hebrew and the Masoretes' reading often swap the words "afflicted" (ani) and "humble" (anav) (Psalm 9:12; Psalm 9:18; Psalm 10:12).
sections.refs: Psalm 9:9; Psalm 9:12; Psalm 9:18; Psalm 10:8–14; Psalm 12:5; Psalm 14:4–6

sections.b: Two early psalms end with seeing God: "those who are upright will look upon his face" (Psalm 11:7), and "I will be filled with the sight of your form" (Psalm 17:15). At the temple, to "see God's face" meant to come into his presence in worship. The word "form" (temunah) recalls Moses, who saw the LORD's form (Numbers 12:8). The Greek softened Psalm 17:15 to "when your glory appears." Christians read both lines with Matthew 5:8 and 1 John 3:2.

Psalm 17:8 is the first of several psalms that ask for shelter in the shadow of God's wings (Psalm 36:7; Psalm 57:1; Psalm 61:4; Psalm 63:7; Psalm 91:4). The image is a mother bird (Deuteronomy 32:11; Matthew 23:37), and perhaps also the cherubim's wings over the ark (1 Kings 6:23–28). The same verse asks God to guard the psalmist "like the pupil of the eye," the phrase of Deuteronomy 32:10.
sections.refs: Psalm 17:8; Deuteronomy 32:10–11; Ruth 2:12; Psalm 36:7; Psalm 91:4; Matthew 23:37

sections.b: Among the marks of the LORD's guest is that he "lends his silver without charging interest" (Psalm 15:5), the law of Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:35–37 turned into a test of character. Loans in Israel were mostly to neighbors in need, so interest meant profiting from hardship. Christian churches long applied the verse to all interest; Calvin and later teachers distinguished oppressive lending from fair commercial interest.

Psalm 14:1–3 pictures the LORD looking down from heaven and finding no one who does good, "no, not a single one." Paul makes it the start of his proof that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin (Romans 3:10–12), and Christian teaching on universal sinfulness has leaned on it ever since. In the psalm itself, the "all" are the fools who devour God's people, set against "the circle of the righteous" (Psalm 14:5); Jewish readers keep that contrast.

sections.h: 'There is no God': practical atheism (Psalms 10 and 14)
sections.b: "There is no God" appears in Psalm 10:4 and Psalm 14:1. The speaker is not a philosopher but the wicked man or the fool (naval), who lives as if God forgets and never looks (Psalm 10:11). The psalms answer with God's seeing and judging (Psalm 10:14; Psalm 14:2). Anselm of Canterbury began his famous argument for God's existence from the fool of Psalm 14:1, a use the psalm did not intend.

Psalm 1 speaks the language of Proverbs: two ways, the advice of the wicked, the mockers, the tree and the chaff (Psalm 1:1–4; compare Proverbs 4:14–19). Most scholars count it among the wisdom or torah psalms, written by the teachers who shaped Israel's prayer book. Its "happy" (ashrei) is a wisdom word (Proverbs 3:13; Proverbs 8:34).
